### Content Service — Runtime
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/content-service/content-service-runtime.json` · per-cluster board: [Content Service — Runtime](/d/apps-v2-content-service-runtime)

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description: CPU seconds burned per second, per pod. 1.0 means one core fully occupied. Read this against the container CPU limit on the row below rather than against the node: extraction runs many documents at once per pod (EXTRACTION_MAX_CONCURRENCY in the applications chart), so a pod can want far more CPU than it is allowed and the excess shows up as throttling, not as a higher line here.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory
panels.description: RSS as the kernel sees it. This is the number that gets compared with the container memory limit by the OOM killer, and it includes what the Go runtime has not yet returned to the OS — so it sits above heap in-use and falls more slowly.

panels.title: Process Virtual Memory
panels.description: Address space reserved, not memory used. Go reserves large arenas up front, so this is normally flat, large, and uninteresting — it is here to distinguish a genuine allocation climb (resident rises with it) from an address-space artefact (only this rises).

panels.title: Container CPU vs limit
panels.description: cgroup CPU usage against the configured limit. The limit is plotted from kube-state-metrics rather than drawn as a fixed threshold, so it follows a helm change on the next rollout instead of going stale — the value itself lives in contentService.resources in the applications chart. Requests and limits are set equal for this service, so there is no burst headroom above the line.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set) vs limit
panels.description: Working set against the memory limit — the pair the OOM killer acts on. Worth watching closely here, because the two limits are not treated alike: the runtime sizes GOMAXPROCS from the cgroup CPU quota on its own, but nothing does the same for memory — GOMEMLIMIT defaults to unlimited and neither the binary nor the chart sets it, so the GC will grow the heap toward the cgroup ceiling without ever knowing it is there. A whole document is held in memory while it is extracted and compressed, so headroom is consumed by document size times concurrency, not by steady-state load. Requests equal limits for this service, so the limit line is also the guaranteed allocation.

panels.title: CPU throttling (share of periods)
panels.description: Fraction of CFS periods in which the container was throttled. Anything sustained above zero means the pod is being held below the CPU it is asking for, which lengthens every latency panel on the other content-service dashboards without producing a single error. Expect this to be the first thing that moves when extraction concurrency is raised.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~".*content-service.*", container="content-service"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~".*content-service.*", container="content-service"}[5m])), 1)

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Goroutine count tracks in-flight work: NATS handlers, both gRPC servers, upload streams and every admitted extraction hold goroutines. It should rise with load and come back to the same floor afterwards. A floor that steps up after each load period and never returns is the leak signal — an extraction that outlived its caller, or a stream that was never closed.

panels.title: Heap In-Use
panels.description: Live heap. Compare its shape with resident memory on the row above: heap that falls while RSS stays high is memory the runtime is holding rather than leaking, whereas both climbing together is the path to an OOM kill.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: GOMAXPROCS vs CPU limit
panels.description: How many OS threads the Go scheduler will run in parallel, against how much CPU the cgroup actually allows. The module is on go 1.26, so the runtime reads the cgroup CPU quota itself and re-checks it periodically: GOMAXPROCS should sit at the CPU limit rounded up and follow a limit change without a restart. Divergence is the finding. A line pinned to the node core count instead means the container-aware default was switched off (GODEBUG containermaxprocs=0, or an explicit GOMAXPROCS env var), and the scheduler is then sizing itself for a machine far larger than the slice the pod owns — which turns into throttling on the row above rather than into more work done. The two series measure different things (threads against cores) and are plotted together only because the gap between them is the point.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Every S3 call, NATS connection, inbound gRPC stream and connector transfer holds a descriptor, so this is the real ceiling on concurrent work per pod. The gap between the two lines is the headroom; open climbing toward max while throughput is flat means descriptors are not being released.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description: Threads the runtime has created. Blocking syscalls — S3 reads, compression, extractor calls — each pin a thread for their duration, so this rises above GOMAXPROCS under load. A ratchet that never comes down usually means threads parked in blocking calls that are not completing.

panels.title: Pods scraped (fleet size)
panels.description: How many content-service pods Prometheus is currently scraping. This deployment is KEDA scaled, so the count moves on its own: scale-up appears here and as new series everywhere else on this dashboard, and it is not a restart. Read the per-pod panels above against this — a fleet sum such as extraction slots in use only makes sense divided by the number of pods reporting.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start. Shutdown here is deliberately slow — the drain budget and the pod's termination grace period are both sized for the longest extraction that can still be running when SIGTERM lands (shutdownTimeoutSeconds and terminationGracePeriodSeconds in the applications chart) — so a rolling update shows a long overlap of old and new pods rather than a clean swap. A sawtooth with a short period is a crash loop, not a deploy.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h increase)
panels.description: Restarts of the container inside an existing pod. KEDA replacing pods does not appear here — that is the fleet-size panel — so anything on this one is the container itself dying and being restarted in place.

panels.title: OOMKilled (last termination)
panels.description: Reads 1 while the last termination of that container was an OOM kill. This is a state, not a counter: it stays at 1 until the pod is replaced, and a pod that has never terminated reports nothing at all. Paired with the memory-vs-limit panel it separates the two ways this service dies — killed for exceeding the cgroup limit, versus exiting for any other reason.

### Authz Service — Overview
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/authz-service/authz-service-overview.json` · per-cluster board: [Authz Service — Overview](/d/apps-v2-authz-service-overview)

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: Pods scraped. The UI manages datasource grants and credentials through this service. nxmain and the nx-pipeline API also ask it whether a user may query a datasource, which fields they see and which datasources they can list, but only when their client.mode is authz-service; in local mode they keep their own checks and never call it. With every pod down, callers in authz-service mode fall back to their own checks, which do not know the datasources this service owns, and the UI's grant and credential screens fail outright.

panels.title: Pods Ready
panels.description: Pods passing /readyz, from kube-state-metrics. Readiness checks every dependency the pod was configured with: nx-backend's database, the JWKS, and, when set, nx-pipeline's database and this service's own. A pod Up here but not Ready is running and scraped while the Service sends it nothing: the readiness log line names the failing check. Not filtered by Pod: that list only holds pods that have been scraped, which would hide exactly the pod stuck in its migrations init container or crashlooping before /metrics.

panels.title: RPC Rate (5m)
panels.description: RPCs per second across all of AuthzService, refused calls included. Every RPC is unary and served over Connect, and the metrics interceptor runs before the token check, so a call refused for its token is counted too. Probes and scrapes are not RPCs and are not in it. With callers in client.mode local, nothing from the query path arrives and this is UI traffic alone, so a near-zero rate is configuration, not an outage.

panels.title: Server Faults % (5m)
panels.description: Share of RPCs that failed on this side: Unknown, DeadlineExceeded, ResourceExhausted, Internal, Unavailable or DataLoss. Unavailable is the common one, and it has two causes that look alike here: a dependency down (a database, auth-service, the credential manager), and a dependency not configured at all. Without NX_PIPELINE_DB_NAME, AUTHZ_DB_NAME or the credential manager, the RPCs that need them answer Unavailable on every call, so a steady non-zero floor since a rollout is configuration; Errors by RPC & Code says which RPCs.

panels.title: Auth Refusals % (5m)
panels.description: Share of RPCs refused as Unauthenticated (no token or API key, or one that failed verification) or PermissionDenied (an unknown or inactive user, or a caller not allowed the RPC). Kept apart from faults because some is normal. A sudden wall of Unauthenticated across every RPC is the JWKS or the API key, not callers: check Pods Ready, which drops with the JWKS. A denial is not an error. CanQuery, HasPermission and IsDatasourceMember answer a refused caller with allowed=false and code 0, so a user being told no counts as OK everywhere on this board.

panels.title: RPC p95 (5m)
panels.description: 95th-percentile RPC duration. In client.mode authz-service, nxmain and the nx-pipeline API bound each call at client.timeoutSeconds (2s in the chart) and fall back to their own checks when it fails, so a tail approaching 2s means callers are quietly answering for themselves, not that users are waiting longer. In local mode there is no caller timeout or fallback: the only callers are the UI, and a slow tail is users waiting. Empty while no RPC arrives in the window.

panels.title: Request Rate by RPC
panels.description: One series per RPC. The method label is the Connect procedure, and only procedures in the proto reach the interceptor (an unknown path is a 404 from the mux), so the series count is bounded by the 22 RPCs. With callers in client.mode authz-service, expect CanQuery, GetFieldPolicy and GetPrincipal to dominate: nxmain and the nx-pipeline API ask them on the query path. In local mode they never call, so only the UI's datasource-management and credential RPCs appear, and those are rare.

panels.title: Request Rate by Code
panels.description: Every RPC by its result code, OK included. Grouped by code, never by the status label beside it, which is free text. A denial is not an error. CanQuery, HasPermission and IsDatasourceMember answer a refused caller with allowed=false and code 0, so a user being told no counts as OK everywhere on this board.

panels.title: Duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
Trustworthy percentiles: the service passes SubsecondLatencyBuckets to the gRPC set explicitly, so the ladder runs 0.005s to 10s rather than the OTel SDK default tuned for milliseconds. In client.mode authz-service, nxmain and the nx-pipeline API bound each call at client.timeoutSeconds (2s in the chart) and fall back to their own checks when it fails, so a tail approaching 2s means callers are quietly answering for themselves, not that users are waiting longer. In local mode there is no caller timeout or fallback: the only callers are the UI, and a slow tail is users waiting.

A call that never returns is never observed, because the histogram records on return, so it moves nothing here: it shows only on RPCs In Flight.

panels.title: Duration p95 by RPC
panels.description: Which RPC is slow. The query-path RPCs read nx-backend's and nx-pipeline's databases; the credential RPCs call the credential manager, bounded by CREDENTIAL_MANAGER_TIMEOUT, so they sit on a different timescale and should not be read against CanQuery.

panels.title: Error Ratio (non-OK)
panels.description: Share of RPCs answered with any non-OK code, with the server-fault share as a second line. The gap between them is callers being refused or rejected, which Errors by Class splits out. clamp_min keeps both ratios defined while the service is idle.

panels.title: RPCs In Flight
panels.description: RPCs being handled right now, by RPC. Calls take milliseconds, so a 30s scrape reads 0 almost always, and that is correct. What this catches is a call that never returns, which no other panel can show: a value that climbs and does not come back down, usually a database or the credential manager holding a connection open.

panels.title: Errors by RPC & Code (rate)
panels.description: Which RPC is failing, and how. Codes: 1 Canceled, 2 Unknown, 3 InvalidArgument, 4 DeadlineExceeded, 5 NotFound, 6 AlreadyExists, 7 PermissionDenied, 8 ResourceExhausted, 9 FailedPrecondition, 10 Aborted, 11 OutOfRange, 12 Unimplemented, 13 Internal, 14 Unavailable, 15 DataLoss, 16 Unauthenticated. 2 is any error that is not a Connect error, so an unexpected failure usually lands there. A single RPC at a steady 14 since a rollout is a dependency it needs that is not configured; every RPC at 16 at once is token verification.

panels.title: Error Ratio by RPC (non-OK)
panels.description: Error Ratio split by RPC. Read it with the rate beside it: the UI's RPCs are called a handful of times, so one refused call is a large share. A high ratio on a tiny rate is a single refusal, not an outage. An RPC with no errors in the window draws no line.

targets.expr: label_replace(sum by (method) (rate(grpc_requests_total{job=~".*authz-service.*", namespace="$namespace", code!="0"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (method) (rate(grpc_requests_total{job=~".*authz-service.*", namespace="$namespace"}[5m])), 0.0001), "rpc", "$1", "method", "$authz_rpc_regex")

panels.title: Errors by Class
panels.description: Non-OK split three ways. Auth refusals are the caller's identity: no or bad token, an unknown or inactive user, or a caller not allowed the RPC. Rejected requests are the request itself: bad arguments, a missing datasource or credential, a write that conflicts, or the caller giving up (Canceled, which is what a caller's own timeout looks like from here). Server faults are this service or what it depends on.

panels.title: Pods Ready vs Pods Up
panels.description: The two lines diverging is a pod running and scraped but out of the Service, because /readyz is failing on one of its dependencies. Readiness is not liveness: such a pod is not restarted, it just stops receiving calls, so a gap that persists is a dependency that stays down. Not filtered by Pod: that list only holds pods that have been scraped, which would hide exactly the pod stuck in its migrations init container or crashlooping before /metrics.

panels.title: RPC Rate by Pod
panels.description: Which replicas callers are reaching. A pod that is up but receiving nothing is out of the Service, usually not Ready.

panels.title: Server Faults by Pod
panels.description: One pod faulting while its peers are clean is that pod's connections or configuration, not the dependency.

panels.title: p95 by Pod
panels.description: A single slow pod points at its own pool or node rather than the database.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, pod) (rate(grpc_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*authz-service.*", pod=~"$authz_pod", namespace="$namespace"}[5m])))

panels.title: In Flight by Pod
panels.description: Where a stuck call is. Normally 0 on every pod.

### Authz Service — Runtime
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/authz-service/authz-service-runtime.json` · per-cluster board: [Authz Service — Runtime](/d/apps-v2-authz-service-runtime)

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description: A request-path service with no background work: every CPU second is an RPC being answered, mostly database reads on the query path. CPU that rises without the RPC rate on the overview board is worth a look at GC Pause and Heap In-Use.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description: Pinned to container="authz-service" rather than container!="". The pod carries a migrations init container, and a per-pod sum over every container folds the schema migration's startup burn into the service's own line, which reads as a CPU spike on every rollout when it is the migration running once.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description: The container limit, not the Go heap, is what the kernel kills on. Compare against Heap In-Use below: a gap that grows without the heap growing is off-heap, and a limit breach shows up here as a restart annotation rather than as anything in the Go panels.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: No background workers beyond the JWKS refresh and the connection pools, so above the idle floor there is about one goroutine per in-flight RPC. A floor that climbs and does not recede is a call that never returns; RPCs In Flight on the overview board says which RPC.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Sockets here are three Postgres pools (nx-backend, nx-pipeline and this service's own, each capped by its *_MAX_CONNS), the auth-service and credential manager clients, the JWKS fetch and inbound Connect calls. A climb that never recedes is a connection not being returned.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start. The service holds no state of its own between calls, so a restart loses nothing but the calls in flight; callers in authz-service mode answer for themselves while no pod is Ready.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h increase)
panels.description: Counts the whole pod, init container included, so a crashlooping migration shows here even though it never reaches the panels above.

### Credential Manager — Overview
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/credentialmanager/credentialmanager-overview.json` · per-cluster board: [Credential Manager — Overview](/d/apps-v2-credentialmanager-overview)

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: Connectors reach this service over gRPC on GRPC_PORT. A pod that is down is a credential lookup failure for every connector; the gRPC row below is that surface's own RED signals.

panels.title: JWKS Available
panels.description: 1 while the JWT authority key set is loaded, 0 while it is unreachable or empty. Zero does not mean this service is down: the gRPC CredentialService that connectors depend on never touches the JWKS, and this is deliberately kept out of the health probes so Kubernetes does not restart the pod or pull it from the Service over it. What it does mean is that every request to the UI-facing Connect API is being rejected, while the gRPC panels below should be entirely unaffected.

panels.title: Admin API Requests (5m)
panels.description: Requests to the UI-facing Connect API, health and metrics endpoints included.

panels.title: Admin API Errors (5m)
panels.description: Non-2xx responses over the last five minutes.

panels.title: Unauthorized (5m)
panels.description: 401 and 403 together. A sustained climb with JWKS Available at 0 is the signature of a JWT-authority outage rather than a caller problem.

panels.title: In Flight
panels.description: HTTP requests currently being served.

panels.title: JWKS Availability
panels.description: keyfunc does not fail when the JWKS host is unreachable -- it serves an empty key set and retries in the background -- so this gauge is the only signal that the UI-facing API is rejecting everything. Alert on it here: it is deliberately not a health check, because a 503 on /health restarts the pod and an unready pod leaves the Service, cutting off the connector gRPC API over a dependency none of them use.

panels.title: Rejected Requests vs JWKS
panels.description: Overlays the 401/403 rate on the gauge. The two moving together is a JWKS outage; 401s without it are ordinary bad tokens.

panels.title: Request Rate by Method
panels.description: GetConnectorCredential is the hot path: every connector calls it to resolve a datasource credential before it can read anything.

panels.title: Errors by Code
panels.description: code="0" is OK and is excluded. code="5" (NotFound) is a connector asking for a credential that was never provisioned, which is a configuration problem rather than a fault here.

panels.title: Duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: On the SubsecondLatencyBuckets ladder. A connector blocks on this call before it can fetch anything, so latency here is latency for every scan.

panels.title: Error Ratio (non-OK)
panels.description: Share of calls returning a non-OK code.

panels.title: In Flight
panels.description: Concurrent calls being served.

panels.title: Request Rate by Route
panels.description: Per-route throughput. The Connect RPCs share one path prefix.

panels.title: Request Rate by Status
panels.description: 401 and 403 separate out the authentication and authorization failures.

panels.title: Duration p95 by Route
panels.description: Buckets are the SubsecondLatencyBuckets ladder this service opts into, so percentiles are meaningful rather than interpolated inside a single bucket.

panels.title: Error Ratio (non-2xx)
panels.description: Share of responses that are not 2xx.

panels.title: Payload Throughput
panels.description: Request and response bytes. Credential writes carry an opaque Any, so a sudden change in request size is worth a look.

panels.title: In Flight
panels.description: Concurrent requests being served.

panels.title: Request Rate by Pod
panels.description: Uses the $credmgr_pod variable; the aggregate panels above deliberately ignore it.

panels.title: JWKS Availability by Pod
panels.description: A single pod reporting 0 is that replica's keyfunc, not the authority being down.

### Datasource Service — Overview
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/datasource-service/datasource-service-overview.json` · per-cluster board: [Datasource Service — Overview](/d/apps-v2-datasource-service-overview)

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description: The UI reaches this service over Connect for everything to do with job definitions, and its schedules fire from the same process. A pod that is down means no scan can be defined, edited or started, and no cron schedule fires for as long as it stays down.

panels.title: API Enabled
panels.description: 1 when this process mounts the Connect API, 0 when it runs the scheduler only. This is the panel that catches a mistyped JWKS_URL: an unset or unusable value turns the API off rather than stopping the process, so the pod starts, passes both probes, keeps firing its schedules, and answers every RPC the UI makes with a 404. Nothing else in the stack reports that — 0 here on a pod meant to serve the UI is the alert.

panels.title: JWKS Available
panels.description: 1 while the JWT authority key set has usable keys. The key set refreshes in the background rather than failing, so a pod that cannot reach its JWKS rejects every token silently — the same gauge Credential Manager exports, for the same reason. Zero here does not stop schedules firing: cron runs inside the process and never presents a token, so expect the firing panels below to keep moving while every UI call is rejected.

panels.title: Firings (5m)
panels.description: Every firing, scheduled and manual, whatever became of it. Skipped and failed firings are counted after their run row is written, so those agree with ListRuns. A submitted firing is the job engine's record rather than a run row, and a not_run firing leaves no record at all.

panels.title: Skipped (5m)
panels.description: A skipped firing is the rule that a definition never runs twice at once, working — not a fault. The definition's schedule came due, or someone pressed Run now, while a ScanStart job, or a job whose kind could not be read, was still active on the datasource access. Deliberately not coloured as an error. Skips climbing while submissions fall is the signal to read the Skip Reasons panel: it usually means a schedule fires faster than its scans complete.

panels.title: Failed (5m)
panels.description:
Firings that were attempted and produced no job, with a run row saying why:

- pipeline_unavailable: the definition has no pipeline, and the connector's scan pipeline could not be resolved or created.
- datasource_unavailable: the access's datasource is not recorded on the definition and could not be looked up.
- invalid_definition: the definition holds a reserved key the job would drop.
- job_engine_rejected: the job engine refused the submission.
- submission_unknown: the submission's result could not be read, so the job may exist.

Unlike a skip, nothing ran, and a scheduled firing does not retry until its schedule next comes due.

panels.title: Not run, faults (5m)
panels.description: Firings that ended before they could run or be recorded, for a reason that is a fault: abandoned, store_unavailable, record_failed or dependency_unavailable. They leave no run row, so this is the only place they appear. The benign reasons, inactive and deleted, are left out so a routine definition edit does not colour this tile; Not-run Reasons shows every reason.

panels.title: API Request Rate (5m)
panels.description: Connect requests per second across JobService, OverviewService, AccessService and ConnectorService, CORS preflights left out. Only the Connect handlers are instrumented, so probes and scrapes are not in it.

panels.title: API 5xx % (5m)
panels.description: Share of Connect requests answered 5xx: server faults, chiefly Unavailable (503) when the job engine, authz-service, request-service or registration-service cannot be reached. Client refusals (400, 401, 403) are not counted here; see Errors by Status Class.

targets.expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS", status=~"5.."}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m])), 0.0001)

panels.title: API p95 (5m)
panels.description: 95th-percentile Connect request duration, CORS preflights left out. RunJobNow and the overview listings call other services, so they set the tail.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m])))

panels.title: Firings by Outcome (rate)
panels.description: submitted, skipped, failed and not_run, the four outcomes a firing can have. Read them together: total firings holding steady while submitted falls and skipped rises is not a fault, it is scans taking longer than the interval between them.

panels.title: Firings by Trigger (rate)
panels.description: schedule is the scheduler firing a due schedule; manual is a RunJobNow call, the UI's Run now. RunAugmentScan starts its job without a firing and is not counted. Scheduled firings should be a regular comb whose spacing matches the cron expressions in use. Every replica polls Postgres for due schedules every 30 seconds, so a flat line at zero while definitions carry enabled schedules means no pod is running, or the scheduler's own reads are failing (logged as "scheduler tick failed").

panels.title: Outcome Share
panels.description: The same four outcomes as a share of all firings, which is what makes them comparable across a quiet period and a busy one. clamp_min keeps the ratio defined when nothing is firing rather than returning NaN and breaking the stack.

targets.expr: sum by (outcome) (rate(job_firings_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace"}[5m])) / clamp_min(scalar(sum(rate(job_firings_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace"}[5m]))), 0.001)

panels.title: Why Firings Are Skipped, Failed or Not Run
Skip Reasons (rate)
panels.description: scan_in_progress is the only skip: a ScanStart job was already active on the datasource access when the firing came due. A job whose kind could not be read blocks the same way and is recorded under the same reason, since a job nobody can classify is still running against the datasource. Usually it is the definition's own previous scan still running; it can also be a scan some other service started on the same access, which the job engine reports just the same. Augments and connection tests never cause a skip. It is policy, not error — what matters is the trend, because a skip that never clears means a schedule is set faster than its scans take.

panels.title: Failure Reasons (rate)
panels.description:
- pipeline_unavailable: the definition has no pipeline, and the connector's scan pipeline could not be resolved or created.
- datasource_unavailable: the access's datasource is not recorded on the definition and could not be looked up.
- invalid_definition: the definition holds a reserved key the job would drop.
- job_engine_rejected: the job engine refused the submission.
- submission_unknown: the submission's result could not be read, so the job may exist.

A RunJobNow caller gets the first three as FailedPrecondition (400) and the last two as Unavailable (503).

panels.title: Not-run Reasons (rate)
panels.description:
Firings that ended with no job and no run row:

- inactive: a scheduled firing whose definition was made inactive, or whose schedule was disabled, after the scheduler claimed it. Benign.
- deleted: the definition or schedule was deleted before the firing could read it or write its run row. Benign.
- abandoned: the caller went away, or the firing timed out, before submission.
- store_unavailable: reading the definition or schedule from Postgres failed.
- record_failed: the firing produced no job and its run row could not be written, so the skip or failure is missing from ListRuns.
- dependency_unavailable: a RunJobNow call whose pipeline or datasource lookup failed because a service it asks could not answer or refused the token. The caller gets that service's code instead of a run row.

panels.title: Failure Ratio
panels.description: Failed firings as a share of firings that reached a submission decision, submitted plus failed. Skips are left out of both sides: in the numerator they would make a correctly throttled schedule look broken, and in the denominator a burst of them would dilute real failures. not_run is left out of both sides too: it mixes benign reasons with faults, and has its own panel.

targets.expr: sum(rate(job_firings_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", outcome="failed"}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum(rate(job_firings_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", outcome=~"submitted|failed"}[5m])), 0.001)

panels.title: API Enabled
panels.description: Aggregated with min, so one pod dropping to 0 pulls the line down rather than being averaged away by its healthy peers. The per-pod split is at the bottom of this board.

panels.title: JWKS Availability
panels.description: Also aggregated with min. The key set is part of readiness but not liveness: a pod at 0 fails /readyz and leaves the Service, so the UI stops reaching it, but it is not restarted and its scheduler keeps firing, because scheduled firings never present a token.

panels.title: Pods Serving the API vs Pods Up
panels.description: The two lines diverging is the case a single gauge hides: pods running and scraped, but not all of them serving the UI. Since api_enabled is decided once at startup from configuration, a gap that appears after a rollout means the new pods came up with different configuration from the old ones.

panels.title: Request Rate by Route
panels.description:
One series per RPC. The route label is the raw request path, not a pattern: the middleware is mounted on each Connect service's path prefix, so a request for a procedure that does not exist under a prefix (a typo, a stale client, a scanner) is recorded as a 404 under its own route. Real RPCs carry no identifiers, so in normal use the series count is the number of RPCs in the proto, but it is not bounded by it. OPTIONS preflights appear here too, because the middleware wraps outside the CORS handler on purpose: a preflight rejected for a missing allowed header breaks every browser call before it reaches a handler, and instrumented inside the wrapper that outage would leave no trace at all.

OPTIONS is excluded so this counts RPCs rather than round trips: under cross-origin use a browser sends a preflight and then the real call, which would read as double the true rate. Preflights are still counted, and are visible on Request Rate by Status as 204 when allowed and 405 when refused — 405s on a route are the CORS signal to watch, not a general non-2xx rate.

panels.title: Request Rate by Status
panels.description:
Non-2xx here is the UI being refused. Cross-read it against JWKS Availability above: a wall of 401s with that gauge at 0 is a JWT authority outage rather than bad callers.

This panel keeps OPTIONS, unlike the rate-by-route and latency panels beside it. That is where preflights belong: 204 is an allowed one, 405 is a refused one, and a rising 405 line against a route means browsers are being turned away before they reach a handler.

panels.title: Duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
Trustworthy percentiles, which is not automatic: pipeline-lib applies no bucket boundaries for you, and its fallback is the OTel SDK ladder tuned for milliseconds. Against a seconds unit every real request would land in one bucket and every percentile would be interpolation noise. The service passes SubsecondLatencyBuckets explicitly, so the ladder runs 0.005s to 10s.

One failure these cannot show: a request that never completes is never observed, because the histogram records on return. Nothing on this board would move — not the percentiles, not the error ratio, since no status is ever written. A hung request shows only on HTTP In Flight, as a value that climbs and does not come back down.

OPTIONS is excluded. A CORS preflight is instrumented deliberately — a refused one is a 405 and is how a cross-origin outage becomes visible — but an allowed one is a near-zero 204 sharing this route label, which would drag the percentile down towards it. It does not arise in the deployed configuration, where the UI is same-origin through the Kong prefix and no preflight is sent.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m])))

panels.title: Duration p95 by Route
panels.description:
Which RPC is slow. The write paths go through Postgres, and RunJobNow and RunAugmentScan call the job engine as well, so they sit on a different timescale from a list call and should not be read against one another.

OPTIONS is excluded. A CORS preflight is instrumented deliberately — a refused one is a 405 and is how a cross-origin outage becomes visible — but an allowed one is a near-zero 204 sharing this route label, which would drag the percentile down towards it. It does not arise in the deployed configuration, where the UI is same-origin through the Kong prefix and no preflight is sent.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m])))

panels.title: Error Ratio (non-2xx)
panels.description: Share of requests answered outside 2xx, with the 5xx share as a second line. Most non-2xx here are refusals, not faults: Connect answers FailedPrecondition and InvalidArgument with 400 (a skipped RunJobNow, or CreateJobDefinition refused because the access's latest connection test did not succeed), Unauthenticated with 401 and PermissionDenied with 403. Server faults are the 5xx line. Errors by Status Class splits the two over time. clamp_min keeps both ratios defined while the API is idle.

panels.title: Payload Size (request mean, response p95)
panels.description:
Request size is a mean, _sum over _count. Its histogram keeps the SDK default ladder, which ends at 10000 bytes, and scan_config is arbitrary caller JSON, so a request percentile would saturate in +Inf as soon as one grew past it. Response size is a p95 on BodySizeBuckets (256B to 4MB), wide enough for a ListRuns page.

Both histograms count fewer requests than http_requests_total, because a request with no body records no size sample. Do not read their _count series as a request rate.

panels.title: Errors by Route & Status (rate)
panels.description:
Which RPC is failing, and how. One series per route and non-2xx status, so a 404 on GetJobDefinition and a 502 on RunJobNow read as different problems rather than one error ratio. Connect maps its error codes onto HTTP statuses for the Connect protocol the UI uses, so the status here is the RPC outcome, not only transport failure.

OPTIONS is kept, as on Request Rate by Status: a refused preflight is a 405 against the route it was guarding, and that is the CORS signal.

targets.expr: sum by (route, status) (rate(http_requests_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", status!~"2.."}[5m]))

panels.title: Error Ratio by Route (non-2xx)
panels.description: Error Ratio split by RPC. Read it with Errors by Route & Status beside it: on a route called a handful of times in the window one failure is a large share, so a high ratio with a tiny rate is a single refused call, not an outage. A route with no errors in the window draws no line. clamp_min keeps each ratio defined while its route is idle.

targets.expr: sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", status!~"2.."}[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace"}[5m])), 0.001)

panels.title: Connect API — By Service & Status Class
Request Rate by Service
panels.description: Requests per Connect service, taken from the route with label_replace. JobService carries definitions, schedules, runs and the two write RPCs, RunJobNow and RunAugmentScan; OverviewService the dashboard reads; AccessService access registration and users; ConnectorService the connector list and scanner forms. OPTIONS is excluded, as on Request Rate by Route.

panels.title: Errors by Service
panels.description: Non-2xx per Connect service. OPTIONS is kept, as on Errors by Route & Status, so a refused preflight shows as a 405 against its service. Most of these are refusals rather than faults: Errors by Status Class gives the split, Errors by Route & Status the RPC.

panels.title: Duration p95 by Service
panels.description: p95 per Connect service. JobService includes RunJobNow and RunAugmentScan, which call the job engine, so it sits above the read-only services. OPTIONS is excluded, as on Duration p95 by Route.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, service) (label_replace(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*datasource-service.*", pod=~"$datasource_service_pod", namespace="$namespace", method!="OPTIONS"}[5m]), "service", "$1", "route", "/nvisionx\\.datasource\\.v1\\.([A-Za-z]+)/.*")))

panels.title: Errors by Status Class
panels.description: Non-2xx split into client refusals and server faults. 4xx is the caller being refused: 400 is FailedPrecondition or InvalidArgument, which includes a skipped RunJobNow and CreateJobDefinition refused for invalid credentials (no separate series; it shares 400 with every other precondition), 401 a missing or rejected token, 403 a caller not allowed the access, 404 a missing definition, 405 a refused CORS preflight. 5xx is this service or a dependency failing: 500 Internal, 503 Unavailable, such as the job engine refusing a firing or not answering. A wall of 401s with JWKS Availability at 0 is the key set being unreachable, not bad callers.

panels.title: HTTP In Flight
panels.description: Connect requests being handled right now, summed across pods. A request that never completes is never recorded by the duration histogram or the error panels, so this is the only place it shows: a value that climbs and does not come back down. At this traffic the normal value is 0 or 1. The gauge has no route or method label, so OPTIONS preflights are included.

panels.title: Firings by Pod (rate)
panels.description: Where firings originate. Every replica runs the scheduler loop and claims due schedules with a conditional update, so a scheduled firing lands on whichever pod claims it first and an uneven split is normal. A manual firing lands on the pod that served the RunJobNow call.

panels.title: API Request Rate by Pod
panels.description:
Which replicas the UI is actually reaching. A pod that is up and serving the API but receiving nothing points at the Service or its endpoints rather than at the application.

Excludes OPTIONS, matching Request Rate by Route above, so the two panels count the same thing.

panels.title: API Enabled by Pod
panels.description: One pod at 0 while the others are at 1 is that replica's configuration, not the JWKS being down.

panels.title: JWKS Availability by Pod
panels.description: A single pod reporting 0 is that replica's key set, not the authority being down. Every pod at 0 together is the authority.

### Datasource Service — Runtime
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/datasource-service/datasource-service-runtime.json` · per-cluster board: [Datasource Service — Runtime](/d/apps-v2-datasource-service-runtime)

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description: This pod is a scheduler, not a data path: work is handed to the job engine rather than performed here, so the baseline is near-idle and the only regular consumer is the cron tick. Sustained CPU on a service that submits jobs and returns is worth a look at the firing rate on the overview board.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description: Pinned to container="datasource-service" rather than container!="". The pod carries a migrations init container, and a per-pod sum over every container folds the schema migration's startup burn into the service's own line — which reads as a CPU spike on every rollout when it is really just the migration running once.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description: The container limit, not the Go heap, is what the kernel kills on. Compare against Heap In-Use below: a gap that grows without the heap growing is off-heap, and a limit breach shows up here as a restart annotation rather than as anything in the Go panels.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: The scheduler is a single goroutine that fires due schedules one at a time, so the count does not grow with the number of schedules. Above the idle floor there is one goroutine per in-flight Connect request. A floor that climbs and does not recede is a request or firing that never returns.

panels.title: GC Pause (max)
panels.description: Longest stop-the-world GC pause per pod. go_gc_duration_seconds is a Prometheus summary, not a histogram: there is no _bucket series, so histogram_quantile cannot be used here. The Go collector exposes quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 only — there is no 0.99. quantile="1" is the max pause over the runtime's buffer of recent GC cycles, so it reports the worst recent pause rather than a windowed percentile.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description: Sockets here are the Postgres pool, the job engine client and inbound Connect calls. A climb that tracks the firing rate and never recedes is a connection not being returned to the pool.

panels.title: Process Uptime
panels.description: Time since process start, and the panel to read before believing a gap in the firing graphs. Schedules live in Postgres and every replica polls them, so a graceful restart of one pod loses no firing while another is up: a firing already claimed is finished before the process exits. A crash is different. A firing is claimed before it runs, so a pod that dies between the claim and the run loses that one firing; it is not retried. With every pod down, a schedule that came due in the gap fires once when a pod returns and the rest of its missed firings are skipped.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h increase)
panels.description: Counts the whole pod, init container included, so a crashlooping migration shows here even though it never reaches the panels above.

options.content:
### Knowledge Hub (sidecar) — Ingestion
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/knowledge-hub/knowledge-hub-sidecar-ingest.json` · per-cluster board: [Knowledge Hub (sidecar) — Ingestion](/d/apps-v2-knowledge-hub-sidecar-ingest)

panels.title: Documents by Outcome (rate)
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the SIDECAR only: the hub image running as a native sidecar inside `applications-knowledge-service-be-go-*`, reached over loopback. It does every document this platform ingests.
- `succeeded` is the only outcome that wrote a document. `reused` short-circuited on same source_url + same checksum and cost one lock acquisition.
- Read `reused` as saved work, not throughput: leaving it in the same series as `succeeded` would make a redelivery storm look like a capacity increase.
- `cancelled` means the caller disconnected at a checkpoint — knowledge-service giving up, usually its own timeout.

panels.title: Ingest Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
- Admission to terminal outcome, per document.
- Shares a bucket ladder with `knowledge_service_pipeline_ingester_request_duration_seconds` on purpose. Compare them bucket-for-bucket: the GAP is queue and transport, not this service.
- `reused` documents land near zero and pull the p50 down, so read this with the outcome split beside it.

panels.title: Failure Error Codes (rate)
panels.description:
- The classification the caller was handed. Retryability is a property of the class, never of whether the client happened to disconnect.
- `db_unavailable` and `coordination_timeout` are retryable and self-correcting at low rates; a sustained rate means the coordinator pool is the ceiling.
- `malformed_content`, `checksum_mismatch` and `object_too_large` are terminal — retrying those burns the caller's delivery budget for nothing.

panels.title: Reuse & Success Share
panels.description:
- `reused` share rising is redelivery: the same document arriving again with an unchanged checksum. Cheap, but it means work upstream is being repeated.
- `succeeded` share falling while total rate holds is the shape that preceded the 2026-08-26 incident, when the ingester answered `success=false, retryable=false` at 60-550 docs/min and did no real work at all.

panels.title: In Flight vs Queued
panels.description:
- `in_flight` is bounded above by INGEST_MAX_CONCURRENT (10 deployed). `queued` is documents blocked on the admission semaphore.
- In flight pinned at the limit with nothing queued is a busy but healthy sidecar. A rising QUEUE is the point at which raising INGEST_MAX_CONCURRENT — and INGEST_COORDINATOR_POOL_MAX with it — is the remedy rather than more replicas.
- The two never overlap: a document is counted in exactly one of them.

panels.title: Admission Wait p95 by Result
panels.description:
- Waiting is deliberate backpressure, not an error: past the coordinator pool ceiling psycopg raises PoolError, which classifies as a RETRYABLE db_unavailable, so the caller re-sends and adds load to a system already at its limit. Blocking converts that into a queue.
- A `timeout` sample never touched a store — nothing retracted, no ledger row — so it is safe to retry immediately.
- The ladder starts at a 0 bucket so an uncontended admission is distinguishable from one that waited a tenth of a second.

panels.title: Document Lock Wait p95 by Result
panels.description:
- Do NOT read this as capacity. Waiting here means the SAME document is being ingested concurrently — usually a redelivery racing its own original — which is exactly what the per-document coordinator lease exists to serialize.
- Admission and this share ONE budget (INGEST_LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS), so a queued request cannot spend the full budget twice.
- `error` means try_acquire itself raised: pool exhaustion or a lost connection, not contention.

panels.title: Ingest Duration Heatmap
panels.description: - The distribution the percentiles flatten. Two bands usually means two populations — `reused` short-circuits against real ingestions — rather than a bimodal latency problem.

panels.title: Failures by Mutation Phase (rate)
panels.description:
- The metric that says whether a failure was EXPENSIVE.
- `pre_mutation`, `acquire`, `acquire_timeout`, `admission_timeout` touched no store: the prior document is intact and a retry is free.
- `prior_retraction_started` / `new_writes_started` mean prior state was already deleted. The document was retrievable before the attempt and is not now — a retry has to rebuild it.
- `ledger_pending` means the new document is written and READY and only the bookkeeping failed.

panels.title: Rollbacks of Partial Writes (rate)
panels.description:
- Every sample is a document that was mutated and then cleaned up.
- `failed` rising is a dependency problem. `cancelled` rising is callers giving up on us mid-write — check knowledge-service's own timeout before assuming this side is at fault.

panels.title: Ledger Write Failures (rate)
panels.description:
- `op="success"` is the costly one: the document is fully written and READY but the ledger does not say so, so the caller is handed a retryable failure and the WHOLE document is re-ingested to reconcile one row.
- Non-zero here means real work is being redone. It is also invisible everywhere else — the ingestion looks like a failure to the caller and like a success in the stores.

panels.title: Destructive-Phase Failure Share
panels.description: - Share of failures that had already deleted prior state. This is the number to alert on rather than the raw failure rate: a service failing 5% pre-mutation is annoying, a service failing 5% mid-write is losing documents that used to be retrievable.

panels.title: Cached Object Size — p50 / p95
panels.description:
- `stored` is what S3 billed and transferred; `decoded` is what the rest of ingestion actually chews through.
- content-service zstd-compresses the text bucket unconditionally at 10-40x, so without the split the two populations would share one distribution and neither would read.
- A cluster of stored samples against 25 MiB is rejection pressure (INGEST_S3_MAX_OBJECT_BYTES), not a size distribution.

panels.title: Achieved Compression Ratio
panels.description:
- decoded bytes / stored bytes, aggregated. Expect roughly 10-40x on text.
- A ratio collapsing toward 1 means objects are arriving uncompressed — legacy objects with no `codec` metadata key, which is legal but means content-service wrote them by an older path.

panels.title: Cache Read p95 & Error Rate
panels.description:
- Covers the whole read: GET, streaming, checksum compare and zstd decode. Splitting further would need timers around code paths that mostly raise.
- `undecodable_content` at volume is the 2026-08-26 signature: a reader that does not dispatch on the `codec` user-metadata key gets raw zstd bytes and fails every object terminally.

panels.title: Document Bytes Handed to Processing
panels.description:
- `source="cached"` is the V2 path (decoded S3 text); `source="upload"` is a direct upload, which should not occur on the sidecar.
- **Read every stage duration against this.** A slow embedding stage on a 90 MiB document is arithmetic, not a regression.

panels.title: Stage Duration p95
panels.description:
- **Start here when ingestion is slow.** This breakdown exists nowhere else: the caller sees one streaming RPC whose progress frames carry a percentage, not a duration.
- Stages in pipeline order: `parse`, `ontology_infer`, `db_store`, `chunking`, `embedding`, `triple_extraction`, `kg_post`, `finalize`.
- `triple_extraction` normally dominates; descend into the Extraction row below to see whether that is the primary pass or the optional verify/discovery passes, which are the two that can be switched off.

panels.title: Stage Share of Wall Time
panels.description:
- Seconds of work per second, per stage — i.e. how much of the sidecar's concurrent capacity each stage is consuming right now.
- Unlike the p95 next door this is weighted by volume, so a slow stage that runs rarely stays small. It is the panel that answers "what would I optimise", where p95 answers "what is slow".
- The total across stages approximates documents in flight.

panels.title: Processing Duration p95 by Outcome
panels.description:
- DocumentProcessor only, excluding admission, lock and S3 fetch. The gap between this and Ingest Duration on the top row is everything the coordinator does.
- `error` far below `ready` is the healthy shape: failures should be cheap.

panels.title: Records / Chunks / Triples per Document
panels.description:
- What each document actually produced, p50 and p95.
- **A 0-chunk document is not retrievable.** In strict (V2) mode that is a terminal MalformedContentError, so a rise in the p50 sitting at 0 means content is arriving that we cannot chunk.
- Triples at 0 with chunks healthy means extraction found nothing — check the Extraction row rather than assuming failure.

panels.title: Documents In Processing vs Completion Rate
panels.description:
- Stall detection. A flat non-zero in-flight with a completion rate at zero is wedged, not busy — and every histogram goes quiet in that state, so nothing else shows it.
- In-flight is taken inside the per-filename lock, so documents blocked behind a same-filename upload are not counted here.

panels.title: Processing Outcomes (rate)
panels.description:
- `ready` vs `error` leaving DocumentProcessor. Counts documents, not attempts.
- Compare with Documents by Outcome at the top: a document can process to READY and still fail the ingestion at the ledger step.

panels.title: Vector Operation p95

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, operation, status) (rate(knowledge_hub_vector_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar", namespace="$namespace"}[5m])))

panels.description:
- `add_chunks` is the whole embed-and-write stage; `upsert` / `put_vectors` is the write alone, instrumented separately because the Pinecone and S3 Vectors stores LOG AND SWALLOW their write failures.
- That is why `status="error"` on the write operation matters more than it looks: `add_chunks` returns normally in that case and reports success.

panels.title: Chunks Written vs Chunks Produced
panels.description:
- **The silent-data-loss check.** `produced` is what chunking made; `written` is what the vector store acknowledged.
- These should track each other exactly. A persistent gap means writes are being dropped by the swallow described next door, and the documents involved are indexed as READY while being unsearchable.

panels.title: Embedding Batches (rate)
panels.description:
- The embedding stage is one long call from the outside. This is the only evidence a large document is ADVANCING through it rather than hanging.
- A flat rate with `embedding` rising on the stage p95 is a stalled embedding provider.

panels.title: Graph & Database Write p95
panels.description:
- Triple writes and the per-document record store. `add_triples` on Neptune fans out into many round trips; see the Neptune panel on the standalone Overview for the per-request view.
- `store_document` slow with a healthy `query` usually means the shared PostgreSQL is write-saturated by concurrent sidecars, not that this document is unusual.

panels.title: Extraction Phase p95
panels.description:
- The breakdown behind `stage="triple_extraction"`, which is usually the dominant stage.
- `pass1` is the primary guided/dynamic extraction. `pass2` (discovery), `verify` and `tabular` are optional passes — if they dominate, they are the levers.

panels.title: Model Calls by Status (rate)
panels.description:
- Extraction fires many short prompts per document, so this rate is roughly records-per-second, not documents-per-second.
- `error` includes a throttle that exhausted botocore's adaptive retries; a rise here with rising stage p95 is Bedrock quota, not model latency.

panels.title: Tokens per Second
panels.description: - Ingestion token spend. Multiply by the per-model rate for cost; the model label is what makes that computable from the series alone.

panels.title: Prompt Cache Hit Ratio
panels.description:
- Process-local cache keyed by sha256(model_id + prompt), 2048 entries, FIFO.
- Expected to be LOW: the same record rarely repeats within one ingestion. A high ratio means the corpus is repetitive; a ratio near zero is normal and not a fault.
- Note the cache is per pod, so it resets on every sidecar restart.

### Knowledge Hub (sidecar) — Runtime
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/knowledge-hub/knowledge-hub-sidecar-runtime.json` · per-cluster board: [Knowledge Hub (sidecar) — Runtime](/d/apps-v2-knowledge-hub-sidecar-runtime)

panels.title: Container Memory (working set) per Pod
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the SIDECAR: the hub image running inside `applications-knowledge-service-be-go-*` as an initContainer with `restartPolicy: Always`. Container series are selected by pod name + `container="knowledge-hub-be-go"` because cAdvisor metrics carry no `job` label.
- **This is what the kubelet counts against the 1Gi limit and what triggers an OOM kill.**
- Open issue: every incarnation since ~2026-08-26 starts near 150-200 MiB and climbs monotonically for as long as it lives (peak observed 368.8 MiB). No incarnation has lived long enough to show a plateau — they are all cut short by deploys — so leak vs working set is still undecided.
- Watch ONE incarnation. The growth is invisible across pod restarts, which is exactly why it went unnoticed.

panels.title: Growth Rate (MiB/min)
panels.description:
- `deriv` over the trailing hour. The measured figure during the open investigation was **+1.125 MiB/min** for this container against +0.019 for the knowledge-service worker beside it.
- Sustained positive with a flat document rate is the leak shape. Positive only while throughput rises is a working set.
- Needs an hour of one incarnation to mean anything; it reads as noise right after a deploy.

panels.title: Retained Bytes per Completed Upload

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (deriv(process_resident_memory_bytes{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar", namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$khub_sidecar_pod"}[1h])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(knowledge_hub_ingest_documents_total{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar", namespace="$namespace", outcome="succeeded", pod=~"$khub_sidecar_pod"}[1h])), 0.0001)

panels.description:
- Memory growth divided by the rate of `outcome="succeeded"` ingestions: **how much this process keeps for every document it finishes.**
- Crude arithmetic during the investigation put it at ~63 KiB per completed upload. That number sizes the search; it is not a claim about where it goes.
- This is the panel that decides the question. A figure that FALLS as throughput rises is a working set. A flat, non-zero figure is a per-document leak.
- Meaningless when the success rate is near zero — the denominator collapses. Read it against the Ingestion dashboard's outcome panel.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory vs Working Set
panels.description:
- RSS is what the Python process holds; working set is what the kubelet bills. They should track; a widening gap is page cache, not the interpreter.
- RSS is newly available for this container — before the metrics endpoint was exposed on the sidecar port there was no `process_*` or `python_*` series for it at all, and the cgroup number was the only thing graphable.

panels.title: Sidecar vs Worker — Shared Pod Budget
Memory by Container

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="$namespace", pod=~".*knowledge-service-be-go.*", container!="", container!="POD"})

panels.description:
- Both containers in the knowledge-service pod. The sidecar has been ~92% of the pod total, which is what made a hub memory climb read as a knowledge-service leak.
- Limits are PER CONTAINER — knowledge-service 512Mi, the hub sidecar 1Gi — so a summed pod figure compares against neither.

panels.title: CPU by Container

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~".*knowledge-service-be-go.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[5m]))

panels.description:
- Cores. The hub sidecar is the CPU-heavy one: parsing, chunking and embedding are all synchronous Python on executor threads.
- Throttling shows up as stage durations rising with no change in document size — cross-check the Ingestion dashboard's stage panel.

panels.title: Restarts by Container (1h increase)
panels.description:
- Zero over 24h for this container throughout the memory investigation, which is the main evidence the growth has not yet reached an OOM.
- A sidecar restart breaks in-flight uploads: expect INGESTER_UPLOAD_FAILED retries on knowledge-service rather than abandoned batches.
- Because it is a native sidecar, the worker does not start until this container has Started and is not terminated until the worker exits.

panels.title: Incarnation Age
panels.description:
- Time since this process started. **Read every memory panel against it**: the growth is only visible within a single incarnation, and every incarnation so far has been replaced by a deploy inside about two hours.
- Deciding leak vs working set needs one of these to run for several hours under load.

panels.title: GC Pause p95 by Generation
panels.description:
- Ingestion allocates heavily and in bursts — parsed record structures, chunk lists, triple objects — and a gen-2 collection over that heap stalls the event loop exactly like a blocking call, but attributed to nothing.
- Read with Event Loop Lag below: lag WITH matching gen-2 pauses is memory pressure; lag WITHOUT them is blocking code on the loop.

panels.title: GC Collections (rate)
panels.description:
- Collections per second per generation, from the standard `python_gc_collections_total` collector.
- A rising gen-2 rate alongside rising memory means the collector is running and NOT reclaiming — the strongest available hint that something holds references rather than that allocation simply increased.

panels.title: Objects Collected (rate)
panels.description: - Objects reclaimed per second. Compare with the collection rate: many collections reclaiming few objects is the signature of a growing live set.

panels.title: Uncollectable Objects (rate)
panels.description: - Objects the collector could not free. Should be zero. Non-zero means reference cycles involving objects it cannot reclaim, which would be a direct explanation for the growth.

panels.title: Event Loop Lag — p95 / p99
panels.description:
- One asyncio loop serves every upload stream on this sidecar while ingestion runs synchronously on executor threads. Anything CPU-bound that lands ON the loop delays every in-flight upload at once.
- No individual operation looks slow when this happens: the work still completes, just after the loop is handed back. This is the only series that shows it.
- A scrape of `/metrics` queues behind the loop too, so sustained lag also shows up as scrape timeouts.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description:
- Each streaming ingestion RPC builds its own single-worker ThreadPoolExecutor, so this rises and falls with concurrent uploads.
- **A monotonic climb that survives idle periods is an executor that is not being shut down** — and would be a candidate explanation for the memory growth, since each thread carries a stack.

panels.title: Asyncio Tasks
panels.description:
- Tasks alive on the loop, which is the streaming layer's own queue depth: RPCs in flight plus the progress-drain machinery behind them.
- Should track ingestions in flight. Growing without them is leaked tasks.

panels.title: Ingest Slots — In Flight vs Queued
panels.description:
- Repeated from the Ingestion dashboard because memory is expected to scale with CONCURRENT documents, not with cumulative ones.
- Memory rising while this stays flat is the observation that makes a working-set explanation hard to sustain.

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description: - Cores consumed by the hub process itself, as opposed to the cgroup figure above.

panels.title: Open vs Max File Descriptors
panels.description: - Each in-flight upload holds an S3 connection and a coordinator connection. A climb tracking uptime rather than concurrency is a descriptor leak.

panels.title: Ingestion Throughput (context)
panels.description: - Present so every memory panel above can be read against load. The regime change in the open investigation coincided with the SUCCESS path starting to run at volume — request volume actually FELL across the transition.

panels.title: Cumulative Documents This Incarnation
panels.description:
- Documents completed since this process started. The investigation's per-upload arithmetic used ~1,870 completed uploads against +115 MiB.
- Plot against working set: a straight line through the origin is a per-document leak, a curve that flattens is a working set reaching steady state.

### Knowledge Hub (standalone) — Overview
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/services/knowledge-hub/knowledge-hub-standalone-overview.json` · per-cluster board: [Knowledge Hub (standalone) — Overview](/d/apps-v2-khub-standalone-overview)

panels.title: Pods Up
panels.description:
- This dashboard covers the STANDALONE deployment only: `applications-knowledge-hub-be-go-*`, the pod serving the Connect API behind Kong.
- The selector `job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go"` has no trailing `.*`, and Prometheus matchers are fully anchored, so it deliberately EXCLUDES `...-knowledge-hub-be-go-sidecar`.
- The same image also runs as an ingestor sidecar inside the knowledge-service pod. That instance does completely different work and has its own two dashboards.

panels.title: RPC Rate
panels.description: All Connect procedures across the four mounted services.

panels.title: RPC p95
panels.description: All procedures pooled. Split by procedure below — a chat stream and a metadata list do not belong in one number.

panels.title: RPC Error Ratio
panels.description:
- Share of calls ending in a Connect code other than `ok`.
- This is the WIRE outcome. A document that failed to ingest but whose stream completed cleanly is `ok` here; that verdict lives on the ingestion dashboard.

panels.title: Request Rate by Procedure
panels.description:
- One series per fully qualified `service/method`.
- The label set is closed — it comes from the generated method descriptor — so it cannot grow with traffic.

panels.title: p95 by Procedure
panels.description:
- Where user-facing latency actually is. Chat synthesis and knowledge-graph traversal dominate; metadata reads should be milliseconds.
- Buckets run 5ms to 1800s, so a chat stream held open for minutes is still resolvable rather than piling into `+Inf`.

panels.title: Connect Codes (rate)
panels.description:
- `ok` is excluded so a low error rate is still legible.
- `unauthenticated` / `permission_denied` are the auth interceptor. `invalid_argument` is usually a client schema mistake, reclassified from a protobuf decode error by ProtoDecodeErrorMiddleware.
- `unknown` is the one to chase: it means an exception escaped a handler.

panels.title: In Flight by Procedure
panels.description:
- Calls currently executing. This is what separates STALLED from IDLE: a wedged dependency observes no durations at all, so the histograms go quiet and the two look identical.
- A procedure pinned above zero with no completions is the shape to alert on.

panels.title: Vector Search p95

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, backend) (rate(knowledge_hub_vector_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~".*knowledge-hub-be-go", namespace="$namespace", operation="search"}[5m])))

panels.description:
- `operation="search"` only: the read path behind chat and document search. Writes happen on the sidecar, not here.
- `backend` is whichever of chromadb / pinecone / s3vectors this deployment resolved to at startup.

panels.title: Graph Operation p95
panels.description:
- Knowledge-graph reads serving entity context and citation grounding.
- On Neptune, read against Neptune Round Trip next door: a slow operation with fast round trips means we are making too many of them, which is a query-shape problem rather than a Neptune one.

panels.title: Neptune Round Trip p95 & Retries
panels.description:
- One signed openCypher HTTP round trip, timed including retries and backoff sleeps because that is what the caller waits for.
- Retries are counted separately: one slow response and three fast failures with two backoffs are indistinguishable on the duration alone.
- Absent entirely when GRAPH_STORE_BACKEND is the local NetworkX store.

panels.title: Document Database p95 by Operation
panels.description:
- `query` is the SQL-expert path answering analytical questions; `get_schema` feeds the prompt that writes those queries.
- `store_document` should sit near zero here — ingestion runs on the sidecar.

panels.title: Model Call Rate by Status
panels.description:
- Chat synthesis, entity canonicalization and the agent tools all land here.
- `error` counts a call that raised, including a throttle that exhausted botocore's adaptive retries.

panels.title: Model Call p95 by Model
panels.description:
- Three model ids at most: the default (Maverick), the fast one (Scout), and the synthesis model (Claude Sonnet), which is pinned in code rather than by env var.
- Synthesis is one call per query on the critical final answer, so its p95 is most of the user's wait.

panels.title: Tokens per Second
panels.description:
- The cost metric: spend is tokens x per-model rate, and the model label is what makes that computable from the series alone.
- Output tokens bill several times higher than input on every model here, so watch the two separately.

panels.title: Tokens per Call
panels.description:
- Mean tokens per invocation — prompt size rather than volume.
- A step change here with a flat call rate means the prompt got bigger, usually more retrieved context rather than more traffic.

panels.title: Ingestion On This Pod — Expected To Be Idle
Ingest Outcomes (rate)
panels.description:
- **This should be flat at zero.** knowledge-service dials the ingestor sidecar over loopback, so no document should reach the standalone pod.
- Non-zero means something is calling `content.v1.ContentService` through the Service or Kong. Worth knowing: this pod shares no admission budget with the sidecars, and INGEST_MAX_CONCURRENT was sized against the coordinator pool on the assumption it is idle.
- If it is legitimately non-zero, the sidecar Ingestion dashboard's panels all work against this job too — change the selector.

panels.title: Documents In Processing
panels.description: - DocumentProcessor concurrency on this pod. Same expectation as the panel beside it: flat at zero.

panels.title: Event Loop Lag p95 / p99
panels.description:
- One asyncio loop serves every RPC on this pod, so anything CPU-bound that runs ON the loop delays every in-flight call at once — and no individual operation looks slow when it does.
- Sustained lag alongside healthy dependency latencies means blocking code, not a slow backend. Check GC pauses on the Runtime dashboard before concluding either.

panels.title: Resident Memory by Pod
panels.description:
- On the overview because it is half of an open question: the sidecar instance of this same image grows monotonically under real ingest while this one has sat flat (149.4 MiB over an 80-minute window, unchanged to one decimal).
- A climb HERE would break that asymmetry and would be the strongest available clue about the cause. Full breakdown on the Runtime dashboard.
